title: NHC wind speed probabilities for hurricanes gave about half the best-track 34-kt wind frequency north of 30N after day 1, and were too flat south of 30N (2010-2025)
abstract: We verified NHC/CPHC Monte Carlo wind speed probabilities (archived 0.5-degree, 120-hour grids) for 7,396 synoptic times and 604 storms against HURDAT2 best-track wind radii. Primary period 2017-2025; replication 2010-2016. Pooled, the 34-kt probabilities were too low: stated/observed events 0.77 (storm-bootstrap 95% interval 0.72-0.83) in 2017-2025 and 0.81 (0.74-0.89) in 2010-2016. We predicted from earlier track-circle results that hurricane-start probabilities would be too flat relative to weaker systems. The sign was opposite: slope difference -0.075 (-0.149 to -0.005). Latitude controls most of the error. After day 1, for storms at hurricane strength at issue, the ratio was 0.51 (0.46-0.56) north of 30N and 1.10 (1.01-1.20) south of 30N; 2010-2016 gave 0.51 and 1.01. South of 30N the probabilities were too flat (recalibration slopes 1.21-1.35). The high-latitude deficit grew with lead and came mostly from large recurving Atlantic hurricanes. Official forecasts that ended early explained 9-29% of it. Official 34-kt radius forecasts were too small at high latitude in 2017-2025 but not in 2010-2016, while the deficit was the same, so they do not explain it. The data agree with a WSP wind-size treatment that misses wind-field expansion at high latitude, or with best-track maximum-extent radii that overstate the wind area; the reference cannot separate these. Uniform radius scaling changes the pooled level (0.98 at 0.8 times the radii) but not the latitude contrast. Code, plan, aggregate results, hashes and retrieval scripts are included; NOAA raw data stay outside the bundle.

display.caption: Reliability of 120-h cumulative 34-kt wind speed probabilities, closest forecast approach 24-120 h, by strength at issue and point latitude, for 2017-2025 and the 2010-2016 replication. Bars are storm-bootstrap 95% intervals.
Sum of stated 34-kt probabilities divided by observed events (points with p >= 1%), by latitude, lead and strength at issue. Values below 1 mean that the stated probabilities are too low.
Official 34-kt radius forecasts divided by best-track radii. In 2017-2025 they were too small at high latitude; in 2010-2016 they were not, while the WSP deficit was the same.
